text: What is the main role of an Operating System?
explanation: The primary role of an OS is to act as an intermediary between user applications and the raw hardware, managing CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices.

text: Which of the following is an example of a desktop operating system?
explanation: Windows is a desktop/workstation operating system, whereas Android and iOS are mobile OSs.

text: Which operating system is developed by Apple for iPhones?
explanation: iOS is Apple's proprietary mobile operating system designed specifically for iPhone devices.

text: Which OS function organizes and retrieves files?
explanation: File Management oversees directory structures, file allocation, access control, and retrieval on secondary storage.

text: Which operating system is open-source and highly customizable?
explanation: Linux is released under the GNU GPL, allowing users to modify, customize, and compile the kernel for any architecture.

text: What is a process?
explanation: A process is a program in active execution with its own address space, program counter, and resources.

text: Which process management function decides the next process to use the CPU?
explanation: CPU Scheduling selects an executable process from the ready queue and allocates CPU time to it.

text: Which memory management technique uses disk space as extra memory?
explanation: Virtual Memory maps secondary storage space (swap/pagefile) as extensions of physical RAM.

text: Which file operation removes a file?
explanation: Delete removes the directory entry and deallocates the disk blocks associated with the file.

text: What acts as an interface between hardware and the OS?
explanation: A device driver translates generic OS commands into hardware-specific control signals for attached peripherals.

text: Which technique manages print jobs in a queue?
explanation: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) buffers printer jobs in disk queues for sequential processing.

text: Which OS processes jobs in groups without user interaction?
explanation: A Batch Operating System collects similar jobs into batches and processes them sequentially with zero interactive intervention.

text: Which OS allows multiple CPUs to execute processes simultaneously?
explanation: A Multiprocessing OS coordinates multiple physical processors sharing bus, clock, and memory to achieve true hardware parallelism.

text: Which OS manages a group of networked computers as a single system?
explanation: A Distributed Operating System presents multiple autonomous networked computing nodes as a single unified system.

text: RTOS stands for:
explanation: RTOS stands for Real-Time Operating System, designed for environments where response time is bounded by strict timing deadlines.

text: Which OS structure has no well-defined architecture?
explanation: A Simple Structure (e.g. early MS-DOS) lacks distinct boundaries between application software, OS services, and hardware BIOS.

text: Which operating system is an example of a simple structure?
explanation: MS-DOS is a classic example of simple monolithic structure without hardware-enforced protection levels.

text: Which structure divides the OS into multiple layers?
explanation: In a Layered architecture, the OS is decomposed into hierarchical layers where layer N only utilizes services of lower layer N-1.

text: Which OS structure uses dynamically loadable modules?
explanation: Modular kernels (like modern Linux modules) dynamically insert kernel objects at runtime without recompiling the core kernel.

text: VirtualBox is an example of:
explanation: VirtualBox is a Type-2 hypervisor that creates and manages Virtual Machines on top of a host operating system.

text: Which structure contains all services in one large kernel?
explanation: A Monolithic architecture executes all core OS subsystems (VFS, IPC, drivers, networking) inside a single large kernel space.

text: Which OS structure runs non-essential services in user space?
explanation: Microkernels (like Mach or QNX) retain only minimal IPC, memory management, and low-level scheduling in kernel space, running drivers and servers in user space.

text: Which OS structure allows services to be dynamically added to the kernel at runtime?
explanation: Modular structures utilize Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) to extend kernel capabilities dynamically on-demand.

text: Which OS structure organizes components into layers where each layer uses services of the lower layer?
explanation: The Layered approach isolates abstractions such that Layer N calls functions exclusively from Layer N-1.

text: In which era was UNIX introduced?
explanation: UNIX was originally created in 1969-1971 at AT&T Bell Labs by Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and team.

text: Which security mechanism verifies users through credentials?
explanation: Authentication validates the identity of users, processes, or devices through credentials before granting system access.

text: Who created Linux?
explanation: Linus Torvalds announced and released the initial Linux kernel in 1991 while studying at the University of Helsinki.

text: UNIX was originally developed at:
explanation: UNIX was invented at AT&T Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey.

text: Which UNIX component acts as the interface between user and kernel?
explanation: The Shell (e.g. bash, zsh, sh) is a command-line interpreter translating user inputs into system calls executed by the kernel.

text: Which is a key feature of UNIX?
explanation: UNIX was architected from the ground up to support multiple concurrent users sharing system compute and storage resources.

text: Which Linux layer contains device drivers?
explanation: In monolithic Linux kernels, device drivers execute directly within privileged Kernel Space (Ring 0).

text: Linux is licensed as:
explanation: Linux is free and Open Source Software licensed under the GNU General Public License (GPLv2).

text: A company wants a free, open-source operating system for servers, cloud platforms, and development environments, with strong community support and frequent updates. Which OS is most suitable?
explanation: Linux distributions (Ubuntu, RHEL, Debian, Rocky) dominate enterprise cloud, container, and server workloads worldwide.

text: What is the main purpose of a system call?
options: Provide an interface between user programs and the operating system
explanation: System calls serve as the programmatic interface allowing user-space applications to request privileged services from the OS kernel.

text: System calls act as a gateway between:
explanation: Executing a system call triggers a software interrupt/trap that switches CPU execution privilege from User Mode to Kernel Mode.

text: Which mode executes system calls?
explanation: System call service routines execute strictly in privileged Kernel Mode with unrestricted hardware access.

text: Which system call is commonly used to display output on the screen?
explanation: The POSIX write() system call writes bytes from a buffer to a file descriptor (such as STDOUT_FILENO = 1).

text: Which of the following is NOT a type of system call?
explanation: Compilers are user-space software tools, not core OS kernel services managed by direct system calls.

text: A process is:
explanation: A process represents a program loaded into memory and actively executing with assigned CPU cycles and state.

text: Which section of a process contains executable code?
explanation: The Text segment (code segment) holds compiled binary machine instructions of the executable program.

text: Which section stores global variables?
explanation: The Data segment stores initialized and uninitialized (BSS) global and static variables.

text: Dynamic memory allocation occurs in the:
explanation: The Heap segment expands dynamically at runtime when functions like malloc(), calloc(), or new are invoked.

text: Function parameters and local variables are stored in the:
explanation: The Stack allocates activation records containing function parameters, local variables, and return pointers.

text: Which process state indicates that instructions are currently being executed?
explanation: A process in the Running state currently occupies the CPU and is actively executing instructions.

text: A process waiting to be assigned to the CPU is in the:
explanation: Processes in the Ready state are loaded in memory and waiting in the ready queue for the CPU scheduler to allocate core time.

text: Which process state indicates the process has finished execution?
explanation: The Terminated (or exit) state indicates a process has completed execution or aborted, waiting for its parent to collect its exit status.

text: PCB stands for:
explanation: PCB stands for Process Control Block (also task_struct in Linux), storing complete process state metadata.

text: Which PCB field stores the address of the next instruction?
explanation: The Program Counter (PC) stores the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed.

text: Context switching occurs when:
options: CPU switches from one process to another
explanation: Context switching saves the current state of a running process and restores the state of another process to resume execution on the CPU.

text: During a context switch, the process context is saved in the:
explanation: The CPU registers, stack pointers, and program counters are saved into the process's PCB entry in memory.

text: A thread is:
options: A basic unit of CPU utilization
explanation: A thread is a lightweight execution stream comprising a thread ID, program counter, register set, and a stack within a process.

text: Threads of the same process share:
explanation: Peer threads inside the same process share the text section, data section, heap, and open file descriptors.

text: Which threading model maps many user threads to one kernel thread?
explanation: The Many-to-One model maps multiple user-level threads to a single kernel thread via a user-space thread library.

text: Which threading model is used by Linux?
explanation: Linux NPTL (Native POSIX Thread Library) employs a One-to-One threading model mapping each user thread to a kernel task (clone).

text: Which threading model maps many user threads to many kernel threads?
explanation: The Many-to-Many model multiplexes a pool of user threads onto an equal or smaller number of kernel threads.

text: Which of the following is a CPU scheduling criterion?
explanation: Core scheduling criteria include CPU Utilization, Throughput, Turnaround Time, Waiting Time, and Response Time.

text: Throughput refers to:
options: Number of completed processes per unit time
explanation: Throughput measures the rate of work done by calculating the number of processes that complete their execution per unit time.

text: Which scheduling method allows a running process to be interrupted?
explanation: Preemptive scheduling allows the OS kernel or higher-priority tasks to forcibly take the CPU away from a currently executing process.

text: In Non-preemptive scheduling, the CPU is released when the process:
explanation: In non-preemptive scheduling, once the CPU is allocated to a process, it keeps the CPU until it either terminates or yields voluntarily for I/O.

text: FCFS stands for:
explanation: FCFS stands for First-Come, First-Served, executing processes strictly in the chronological order of their arrival in the ready queue.

text: FCFS scheduling follows which queue discipline?
explanation: FCFS operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue discipline.

text: FCFS scheduling is:
explanation: Standard FCFS is non-preemptive; a running process retains the CPU until completion or blocking.

text: SJF stands for:
explanation: SJF stands for Shortest Job First, which schedules the process with the smallest expected CPU burst time first.

text: SJF scheduling selects the process with the:
explanation: SJF selects the process with the shortest CPU burst time, proving mathematically optimal for minimizing average waiting time.

text: The preemptive version of SJF is known as:
explanation: SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First) preempts the running process if a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining burst time.

text: Round Robin scheduling uses a fixed:
explanation: Round Robin assigns a fixed discrete time slice called a Time Quantum (or time slice) to each process in circular order.

text: Round Robin scheduling is a:
explanation: Round Robin is preemptive by design because the timer interrupt forcibly preempts a process when its time quantum expires.

text: A Gantt chart is used to:
explanation: A Gantt chart provides a horizontal timeline bar visualization of CPU scheduling illustrating start, execution, and finish times for processes.
